\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can introduce myself in Sanskrit, give my name, and understand the other person's name.}

Complete SA-C02-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise: introduce myself in Sanskrit, give my name, and understand the other person's name.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nāma]{\sk{नाम} (nāma) — \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} the source of a word half the world shares}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-nama}



\begin{quote}
The first word of the introduction — and, since this is Sanskrit, the \emph{source} of the word half the world uses.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{nā · ma}. A long first beat and a short second — the two vowels English keeps apart in \emph{father} and \emph{sofa}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nāma} (\textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} neuter) is from the stem \emph{nāman}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{3}nomn-}. This is not a \emph{borrowing} from anywhere — it is the ancestor: the same root surfaces as English \textbf{name}, Latin \emph{nōmen} ($\to$ \textbf{noun}, \textbf{nominate}), Greek \emph{onoma}, and, worn down, as Hindi \emph{nām}, Bengali \emph{nām}, Punjabi \emph{nāṁ}. When you say Sanskrit \emph{nāma}, you are standing near the headwaters of a word that flowed to both Europe and modern India.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāma\textquotedblright{}
  \item its children, west and east — English \emph{name}, Latin \emph{nōmen}; Hindi \emph{nām}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What PIE root is \emph{nāma} from, and name two of its descendants. (\emph{*h\textsubscript{3}nomn-}; any two of English \emph{name}, Latin \emph{nōmen}, Greek \emph{onoma}, Hindi \emph{nām}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mama]{\sk{मम} (mama) — \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} the ancestor of \emph{me} and \emph{my}}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-mama}



\begin{quote}
The word that makes the name yours — and it is, quite literally, the grandparent of English \emph{my}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{ma · ma}. Two identical short beats, evenly stressed.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mama} (\textquotedblleft{}my, of me\textquotedblright{}) is the genitive of \emph{aham} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}), on the first-person root \textbf{ma-}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*me-}. This is the source of the whole first-person family: English \textbf{me}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{mine}, Latin \emph{meus}, Greek \emph{emou}, and Hindi \emph{merā}. Sanskrit \emph{mama} and English \emph{my} are not merely similar — they are the same ancient word, one still in its old form, the other worn smooth by five thousand years.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mama\textquotedblright{}
  \item the m- family — \emph{mama} / English \emph{me}, \emph{my} / Latin \emph{meus} / Hindi \emph{merā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{mama} the genitive of, and its English cousins? (\emph{Aham}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}; English \textbf{me}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{mine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ḥ]{\sk{◌ः} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S201-sign-visarga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{न} · \sk{द} · \sk{◌्}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{◌ः}}
\textbf{\sk{◌ः}} — \emph{ḥ}.

It is a \textbf{visarga}: not a letter, but a soft breathed \emph{ḥ} at the end of a syllable. It is the mark that ends a great many Sanskrit masculine nouns, so it is worth knowing on sight.

Where it sits: a pair of dots to the right of the syllable, marking a voiceless post-vocalic breath.

Worked through: \textbf{\sk{न}} + \textbf{\sk{◌ः}} = \textbf{\sk{नः}} — \emph{naḥ}.

You already say these words, and \sk{◌ः} is one of the shapes inside them — the rest of their shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{namaskāraḥ} — hello (lit. \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{dhanyavādaḥ} — thank you
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{◌ः} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \sk{◌ः} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{◌ः} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{◌ः}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{◌ः} three times, saying \emph{ḥ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{◌ः} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{◌ः}? What does it add to the end of a syllable? (\textbf{A soft breathed \emph{ḥ}.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[asti]{\sk{अस्ति} (asti) — \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} the ancestor of \emph{is} and \emph{est}}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-asti}



\begin{quote}
The little verb \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — and here you meet it in the form that fathered half the \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} words on earth.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{as · ti}. The \emph{s} closes the first beat; \emph{ti} follows cleanly after it.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{asti} (\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) is the third-person singular of the root \emph{as-} (\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}), from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}es-}. It is the source of the family's copula: English \textbf{is}, German \emph{ist}, Latin \emph{est}, Greek \emph{esti}, and Hindi \emph{hai} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{asti} directly). Unlike its Dravidian neighbours — Tamil and Bengali drop \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} in the present — Sanskrit \emph{keeps} an explicit copula, and it is the very word Europe kept too.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}asti\textquotedblright{}
  \item the family — \emph{asti} / English \emph{is} / Latin \emph{est} / Greek \emph{esti} / Hindi \emph{hai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \emph{asti} from, and its cousins across the family? (\emph{As-} / PIE \emph{*h\textsubscript{1}es-}; English \emph{is}, Latin \emph{est}, Hindi \emph{hai}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mama nāma … asti]{\sk{मम} \sk{नाम} … \sk{अस्ति} (mama nāma … asti) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-mama-nama-asti}



\begin{quote}
Three atoms you now own, assembled — and note that Sanskrit, unlike Tamil or Bengali, actually \emph{says} the \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mama} (my) + \emph{nāma} (name) + your name + \emph{asti} (is) = \textbf{mama nāma … asti}, \textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{} \emph{Mama nāma Aruṇaḥ asti.} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Sanskrit keeps the \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}}]
Where Tamil says only \emph{eṉ peyar Arun} and Bengali \emph{āmār nām Arun} — both dropping the verb (the zero copula) — Sanskrit says \emph{mama nāma … asti}, with an explicit \emph{asti} (\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}). This is the Indo-European way, the one Latin and English kept too (\emph{my name is …}). The verb comes \textbf{last}, as in the modern Indian languages that descend from it. (In casual use \emph{asti} can be dropped, but the \textquotedblleft{}full-dress\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit sentence keeps it.)
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mama nāma … asti\textquotedblright{} with your name
  \item how this differs from Tamil/Bengali (Sanskrit keeps the \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name in Sanskrit, and say what it keeps that Tamil and Bengali drop. (\emph{Mama nāma … asti}; the copula \emph{asti}, \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\sk{आ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S04-letter-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{द} · \sk{◌्} · \sk{◌ः}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{आ}}
\textbf{\sk{आ}} — \emph{ā}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel}: the full-size letter a vowel wears when it opens a word and has no consonant to lean on. Inside a word the same vowel is written as a small sign instead.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the joined upper-and-lower left body of \emph{a}
  \item a middle shoulder
  \item an inner vertical stem
  \item a trailing vertical stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say this word, and \sk{आ} is one of the shapes inside it — the rest of its shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ām / na} — yes / no
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{आ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the inner stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the trailing stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{5.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 4.} The pen comes up 4 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the shared \emph{a} body into more strokes
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \sk{आ} stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{आ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{आ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{आ} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{आ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhavān]{\sk{भवान्} (bhavān) — the respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-bhavan}



\begin{quote}
To ask someone's name you need a word for \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — and for a first meeting, Sanskrit reaches for the polite one.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{bha · vān}. The \emph{bh} is one sound — a \emph{b} released with breath behind it. The second beat carries a long \emph{ā} and closes on \emph{n}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Bhavān} (\textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} respectful) is not really a second-person word at all: it is a third-person honorific — \textquotedblleft{}your honour,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{bhavat} (\textquotedblleft{}being, gracious one\textquotedblright{}) — and so it takes a \emph{third-person} verb (\emph{bhavān asti}, \textquotedblleft{}your honour is\textquotedblright{}). For a first meeting, use \emph{bhavān}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: politeness by grammatical person}]
Where Hindi and Punjabi make respect \emph{plural} (\emph{āp … haiṁ}), Sanskrit makes it \emph{third-person}: to be polite you address someone as though speaking \emph{about} them — \textquotedblleft{}is your honour well?\textquotedblright{} rather than \textquotedblleft{}are you well?\textquotedblright{} Different trick, same courtesy.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — \emph{bhavān}
  \item what it literally means (your honour)
  \item why it takes a third-person verb (it speaks \emph{about} the person)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Sanskrit build respect into \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} and how does Hindi do it instead? (Sanskrit uses a third-person honorific, \emph{bhavān} \textquotedblleft{}your honour\textquotedblright{}; Hindi uses a plural, \emph{āp}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tvam]{\sk{त्वम्} (tvam) — the familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-tvam}



\begin{quote}
The other \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — the one you use with friends, and the ancestor of English \emph{thou}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{tvam} — one beat. The \emph{tv-} is a single push, \emph{t} and \emph{v} said together, and then the lips close on \emph{m}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Tvam} (familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) is from Proto-Indo-European *\emph{tū} — the direct ancestor of English archaic \textbf{thou}, Latin \emph{tū}, French \emph{tu}, and Hindi \emph{tū}. Unlike \emph{bhavān}, it takes an ordinary second-person verb. Its possessive is \emph{tava} (\textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}), which you will need in the very next question.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item both words for you — \emph{tvam} (familiar), \emph{bhavān} (respectful)
  \item the English cousin of \emph{tvam} (\textbf{thou})
  \item which one you would use on a first meeting (\emph{bhavān})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What English word is \emph{tvam} cousin to, and what is its possessive form? (Archaic \textbf{thou}; \emph{tava} \textquotedblleft{}your.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kim]{\sk{किम्} (kim) — \textquotedblleft{}what,\textquotedblright{} the source of the question-words}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-kim}



\begin{quote}
The question-word — and the fountainhead of a whole family of \textquotedblleft{}wh-\textquotedblright{} words, east and west.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{kim} — one short beat, closing on \emph{m} with no vowel after it.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kim} (\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) is from the interrogative stem \emph{ka-}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — the ancestor of the whole question-family: English \textbf{what}, \textbf{who}, \textbf{which}, Latin \emph{quis} / \emph{quid}, Greek \emph{tis}, and Hindi \emph{kyā} / \emph{kaun}. Sanskrit's own questions all grow from this \emph{ka-}: \emph{kim} (what), \emph{kaḥ} (who), \emph{kadā} (when), \emph{kutra} (where), \emph{katham} (how). It is the single seed from which both Europe's \emph{qu-/wh-} words and India's \emph{k-} words grew.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kim\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ka- family — \emph{kim, kaḥ, kadā, kutra, katham}
  \item its western children (English \emph{what}, Latin \emph{quis})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What PIE root is \emph{kim} from, and its cousins? (\emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}; English \emph{what}, Latin \emph{quis}, Hindi \emph{kyā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bha]{\sk{भ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S202-letter-bha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{◌्} · \sk{◌ः} · \sk{आ}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{भ}}
\textbf{\sk{भ}} — \emph{bha}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{bh}, it is \textbf{bha}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a clockwise upper loop joined to a descending trunk
  \item a clockwise lower bowl continuing through a rightward crossbar
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say this word, and \sk{भ} is one of the shapes inside it — the rest of its shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhavān / tvam} — you
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{भ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the upper loop's lower inner tip, sweep left and clockwise around the upper loop, descend the joined trunk, curl clockwise around the lower bowl, and continue right through the crossbar without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified three-stroke teaching form; another learner source stages the upper and lower body parts separately
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: JackPotte, ‘Devanagari b\textsuperscript{h} \sk{भ}.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{भ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{भ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{भ} three times, saying \emph{bha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{भ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{भ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{bha}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tava nāma kim?]{\sk{तव} \sk{नाम} \sk{किम्}? (tava nāma kim?) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-tava-nama-kim}



\begin{quote}
Turn the introduction around — ask, instead of tell.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tava} (\textquotedblleft{}your,\textquotedblright{} the genitive of \emph{tvam}) + \emph{nāma} (name) + \emph{kim} (what) $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your name what?}\textquotedblright{} Here Sanskrit often \emph{drops} the \emph{asti}: \emph{tava nāma kim?} stands complete, the question-word alone doing the work.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the respectful version}]
\emph{Tava} (\textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}) is the familiar form, matching \emph{tvam}. To a respected stranger, use the honorific: \emph{bhavataḥ nāma kim?} (\emph{bhavataḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}of your honour\textquotedblright{}). Note \emph{mama} / \emph{tava} / \emph{bhavataḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}my / your / your-honour's\textquotedblright{} — all built the same way, as genitives.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the familiar question — \emph{tava nāma kim?}
  \item the respectful version — \emph{bhavataḥ nāma kim?}
  \item answer it — \emph{mama nāma … asti}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{} respectfully, and give the \textquotedblleft{}my/your\textquotedblright{} pair. (\emph{Bhavataḥ nāma kim?}; \emph{mama} \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} / \emph{tava} \textquotedblleft{}your.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ānandaḥ]{\sk{आनन्दः} (ānandaḥ) — \textquotedblleft{}joy,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a joy to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-anandah}



\begin{quote}
The warm close of an introduction — a word so full it names bliss itself.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{ā · nan · daḥ}. Long \emph{ā} to open, \emph{nd} said together in the middle, and the soft breathed \emph{-ḥ} to close.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
To say \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you,\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit can say \emph{bhavantaṁ dṛṣṭvā ānandaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{seeing you, {[}there is{]} joy}.\textquotedblright{} The key word \emph{ānandaḥ} (\textquotedblleft{}joy, bliss, delight\textquotedblright{}) is from \emph{ā-} (\textquotedblleft{}fully\textquotedblright{}) + the root \emph{nand} (\textquotedblleft{}to rejoice\textquotedblright{}). It is one of Sanskrit's most beloved words — the \emph{ānanda} of \emph{sat-cit-ānanda} (\textquotedblleft{}being-consciousness-bliss\textquotedblright{}), and the name \textbf{Ānanda}, the Buddha's devoted disciple. So a simple greeting reaches for the word Indian thought uses for the deepest happiness.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ānandaḥ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the full phrase — \emph{bhavantaṁ dṛṣṭvā ānandaḥ}
  \item where else \emph{ānanda} appears (bliss; the name Ānanda)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ānandaḥ} mean, and what is it built from? (\textquotedblleft{}Joy, bliss\textquotedblright{}; \emph{ā-} \textquotedblleft{}fully\textquotedblright{} + \emph{nand} \textquotedblleft{}to rejoice.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\sk{◌ि} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S109-vowel-sign-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{◌ः} · \sk{आ} · \sk{भ}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{◌ि}}
\textbf{\sk{◌ि}} — \emph{i}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: a curl placed BEFORE (to the left of) the consonant, though pronounced after.

Worked through: \textbf{\sk{न}} + \textbf{\sk{◌ि}} = \textbf{\sk{नि}} — \emph{ni}.

You already say these words, and \sk{◌ि} is one of the shapes inside them — the rest of their shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{asti} — is
  \item \emph{mama nāma … asti} — my name is…
  \item \emph{kim} — what
  \item \emph{tava nāma kim?} — what's your name?
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{◌ि} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \sk{◌ि} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{◌ि} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{◌ि}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{◌ि} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{◌ि} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{◌ि}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{i} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — the whole exchange}

\label{lesson:SA-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Two people meet, and every word in the exchange is one you already have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mama nāma mīrā asti.} — \textquotedblleft{}My name is Mira.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{tava nāma kim?} — \textquotedblleft{}What's your name?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{mama nāma aruṇaḥ asti.} — \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{bhavantaṁ dṛṣṭvā ānandaḥ.} — \textquotedblleft{}Pleased to meet you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{How to answer: the atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item name, my, is, what (\emph{nāma}, \emph{mama}, \emph{asti}, \emph{kim})
  \item where the verb sits in the sentence (last)
  \item whether Sanskrit drops the \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} (no — it keeps an explicit copula)
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: every atom is a source}]
Every word in that exchange is an \emph{ancestor}, not a borrowing:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nāma} $\to$ English \textbf{name}, Latin \emph{nōmen}
  \item \emph{mama} $\to$ English \textbf{my}, \textbf{me}
  \item \emph{asti} $\to$ English \textbf{is}, Latin \emph{est}, Hindi \emph{hai}
  \item \emph{kim} $\to$ English \textbf{what}, Latin \emph{quid}
\end{itemize}

And Sanskrit keeps the copula that its Dravidian neighbours drop. Next chapter: \emph{bhavān katham asti?} — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name in Sanskrit, ask for someone else's, and name two English words this chapter's vocabulary is the ancestor of. (\emph{Mama nāma … asti; tava nāma kim?}; any two of \textbf{name}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{is}, \textbf{what}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
